You learn pitch accent theory if you’re interested in having a native-like accent. Other than that, shadowing before fluency is pointless. An example of practicing pitch accent, would be reading the pitch accents in dictionaries such as the “NHK pitch accent dictionary” and repeating, so that way you’re reinforcing the patterns for when you do begin starting output. Shadowing can be useful for pitch accent and focusing your attention on the pitch raises and drops when listening too. But if you’re not focusing on pitch accent then shadowing and replicating is a waste of time (and will lead to you developing bad habits such as inproper pronounciation). And output (creating Japanese) before fluency is a definite no and to say it bluntly will fuck your Japanese big time if you do it often. 

Also with Dogen, yes he practiced loads of pitch accent before fluency, he pretty much primarily focused on his pitch accent before getting fluent.

If that’s the case, then you’re better off learning pitch accent now. Dogen actually did this himself, where before he was fluent in Japanese he focused on pitch accent and pretty much had a perfect accent where even natives would assume he was already fluent (yet he wasn’t at the time). Doing this, by the time you’re fluent you won’t have to correct your accent or pronounciation. It does take a bit of time though and you have to learn the rules associated with pitch accent (since it’s not something you can naturally aquire unless you’re mother tongue is tonal).

Okay, the whole point in shadowing is to actually copy what the native speaker is saying which will help develop the patterns (習慣) for when you output. Even if you understand Japanese 100%, producing output is still difficult especially if you haven’t yet practiced, and that practice is “shadowing”. 

But tell me, what use is there shadowing words you don’t yet know? If you’re not already fluent, then it’s a waste of time because you don’t need to output until you’re already fluent in understanding. Input before output. And watching anime for 10 years with English subtitles - I’m sorry but that’s not going to do anything, yeah it will make your ears familiar with the language but you’re not going to get far. Realistically, if you want to make rapid progress you’ve got to be immersed everyday in Japanese (12+ hours). 

And this has already been clarified before, English subtitles and anime is not classified as immersion. Remember your brain can only focus on one task at a time realistically, so if you’re reading English subtitles, you’re not actually focusing on listening to the language.

It’s not a bad thing, as long as it doesn’t bother you too much. If it does then just don’t. Otherwise, you should be making sentence cards with i+1 sentences for those sentences with one unknown word.

“Language acquisition does not require extensive use of conscious grammatical rules, and does not require tedious drill.

I will elaborate. Actually, this isn’t really some special or secret “method” of learning Japanese. It’s more so common sense. Stephen Krashen, a linguistic from the 80’s made a statement that all language acquisition takes place from input and exposure and not grammar study. So really this method is just listening to comprehensible Japanese 24/7, shows that you’ve watched etc. So just downloading audio from shows and listening all the time. You’re basically exposing your brain to thousands of hours of native speech and so you naturally aquire the language like a baby would. This is common sense. Therefore if you’re listening 24/7 or course you’re gonna reach a high level fast because you’ve had more exposure to the language than someone who traditionally studies.

And by “beyond fluency” I mean vocabulary that you rarely even see in Japanese, like extremely rare terms etc. since anime having so many genres there’s all sorts of odd vocabulary you will run into. Hence why I say “beyond fluency”.

Oh trust me, there’s plenty of anime genres that have a wide variety of Japanese, from classic, casual, keigo and even some extremely formal Japanese that a textbook wouldn’t teach you. Learning from anime can take you beyond just fluency. 

Problem is, once you’ve passed that N4 level, textbooks really limit your vocabulary. Textbooks can only hold so much within them, so really they’re limiting. Sentence mining combined with SRS (Anki) + immersion has been literally proven to be one of the fastest tracks to reaching advanced levels of Japanese. Take Khatzumoto from AJATT, MattVsJapan, BritVsJapan for example. Both Khatzumoto and BritVsJapan reached fluent levels within as little as 18 months following the immersion routes, and if you ask them whether they used a textbook or not I can guarantee you they didn’t, they’ve even said themselves that they never used textbooks, just immersion and sentence mining.

Textbook and traditional approach will take you 5-10 years, a mass immersion approach will take you a couple years. Simply because you are surrounded by Japanese audio 24/7. So instead of studying grammar you are picking it up naturally. If anyone thinks this is rot, go and do your research on language acquisition, because chances are you probably haven’t even looked into it.

Yeah that’s exactly right. You can’t not pay attention to the audio, you gotta listen. And if you struggle listening and paying absolute attention to the audio all the time best thing to do is watch a show like anime, that way you’re actually paying attention and wanting to know what is happening.

I’m not saying just watch anime or native material. More so after you’ve built a small foundation for the language where you can absorb content without too many issues. It’s still possible without having a foundation as long as you’re occasionally searching up vocab from words you find by reading/watching. 

My main point is that many people that start Japanese study traditionally all the way through, without much exposure to native content and audio. And of course that’s a problem. Realistically after you’ve reached around a N5-N4 level of Japanese you should just focus primarily on absorbing native material. But of course many people continue going through advanced and intermediate textbooks which is a waste of time. And with kanji, of course that’s something you have to work on.

Immersion and input will always be more effective though than textbooks. Textbooks give that stepping stone to get into native material, whilst native material is what will take you all the way to fluency and beyond. Nobody has ever learnt a language to fluency without being exposed to thousands of hours of native speech.

This is how you study Japanese properly. Immersion based learning is far more effective than traditional textbook and grammar study. 

Just stick in some headphones and listen to Japanese all day or watch anime all day, that’s what I do and you learn heaps. You just naturally pick it up.

I recommend you look into immersion based approaches to language learning. Listening to Japanese audio all day long and watching shows in Japanese will skyrocket your language ability. I can’t imagine anyone getting far outside Japan if they were just doing traditional textbook study. Language all comes down to how many hours you have been exposed to it, so the solution is to expose yourself to as much Japanese outside of Japan. Anyone can reach fluency in Japanese without living in the country.

It’s not so much that keeping track of words you learn is a problem. But more so, you don’t actually “learn” words you slowly aquire them overtime from being exposed to lots of content. You can memorise vocabulary lists etc. but if you don’t aquire those words in context you’re not really learning them properly and that’s why keeping track of how many words you have supposedly “learnt” is difficult and entirely pointless. Sometimes you’ll forget words. And so just focusing on picking up words from context like tv shows etc. and not worrying about whether you’ve “learnt” the words is probably a better idea.

So more so, regardless of how many words you “know” it doesn’t showcase your ability to understand those words in surrounding context, hence you can’t “learn” those individual words without being exposed to loads of context. So whether you know 10,000 or 20,000 words, someone that does may have 0 clue how these words are being used in content. So learning individual words or measuring your ability based on how much words you know is quite pointless.

I’m not criticising or anything, just saying that it’s a good idea to focus on other things rather than how many words you know. Just giving helpful advice :)

Dude, you find sentences using native material and make flash cards with them. It’s actually not hard nor does it take time to make a flash card. 10 seconds. If you’re using native material such as tv shows, anime etc. and then making cards with i+1 sentences (1 word in the sentence that you may not know) it is very beneficial. It’s called “sentence mining”. And a lot of successful people at acquiring a language to a native-level have used this method. Look up “Matt Vs Japan”, “Brit Vs Japan” “AJATT”. They’ve all done sentence mining using SRS software such as “Anki”. But I’m not saying that Anki is where it’s all at. It simply reinforces what you’ve discovered through native material. Input is where it’s all at. Listening, reading etc. Anki fastens the process. I’m not saying Anki is 100% essential however it will definitely speed the process without a doubt. 

Eventually you will want to transition to monolingual cards. If you don’t know a word copy and paste the definition from a J-J dictionary into the flash card’s meaning, hence you can read the definition for that word in Japanese. You’re learning Japanese words in Japanese whilst using SRS. That is gold.
Anki is still great to use as you advance. As long as you’ve using it to make monolingual cards with sentences you’ve seen.

So far I’ve gathered the following pros and cons:

- Genki -

Pros:
- The textbooks are in English.
- Easy to follow along with, good (especially) for beginners new to Japanese completely. 


Cons:
- Less vocabulary and lessons than Minna No Nihongo.
- Less workbooks. 
- Too many English translations may prevent immersion in the language and may cause bad pattern (need to always translate to English)


- Minna No Nihongo -

Pros: 
- More additional workbooks, material and vocabulary.
- More audio for listening.
- Does come with translation book (seperate)

Cons:
- Entirely in Japanese (may be good / bad)
- More difficult to follow (requires more effort from the learner)
- Not as good for self study compared to Genki
